concept.name: Bellman-Ford Shortest Paths

relationships.description: Connects Bellman-Ford Shortest Paths to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Bellman-Ford computes single-source shortest paths in $O(VE)$ time by relaxing every edge $V - 1$ times, uniquely supporting negative edge weights and detecting negative-weight cycles.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use Bellman-Ford when edges can have negative weights or when you need to detect negative cycles (such as currency arbitrage); otherwise, Dijkstra's $O((V+E)\log V)$ is far faster.

concept.whyItMatters: Dijkstra's greedy assumption—that once a vertex is popped from the min-heap its shortest path is final—breaks immediately if any edge has a negative weight. Bellman-Ford solves this cleanly and powers both negative-cycle detection in financial/constraint systems and the distributed distance-vector routing family (RIPv2, BGP path-vector concepts).
whenToUse: Directed graphs containing negative edge weights (e.g., rebates, elevation/energy recovery, difference constraints $x_j - x_i \le w$).
Detecting negative-weight cycles, such as currency exchange arbitrage where $\prod r_i > 1$ becomes $\sum (-\ln r_i) < 0$.
Distributed distance-vector routing where nodes only know neighbor distances and converge via iterative relaxation.
whenNotToUse: Graphs with all non-negative edge weights—Dijkstra's algorithm runs in $O((V+E)\log V)$ instead of $O(VE)$.
All-pairs shortest paths on dense graphs—Floyd-Warshall ($O(V^3)$) or Johnson's algorithm ($O(V^2 \log V + VE)$) is better suited.
Unweighted graphs—standard BFS finds shortest paths in linear $O(V + E)$ time.
keyPoints: Core invariant: after $k$ full relaxation passes over all $E$ edges, `dist[v]` holds the shortest path from source $s$ to $v$ using at most $k$ edges.
Because any simple path in a $V$-vertex graph has at most $V - 1$ edges, $V - 1$ passes suffice when no negative cycles are reachable.
Negative-cycle detection: run a $V$-th pass; if any edge $(u, v, w)$ still satisfies `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, a reachable negative cycle exists.
Early-exit optimization: track a `changed` boolean per pass; if an entire pass relaxes zero edges, terminate immediately.
SPFA (Shortest Path Faster Algorithm) queues only vertices whose `dist` improved, averaging $O(E)$ on random sparse graphs while remaining $O(VE)$ worst-case.

examples.title: FX Currency Arbitrage Detection
examples.scenario: A trading engine models 30 currencies as vertices and exchange rates $r_{u,v}$ as directed edges with weight $-\ln(r_{u,v})$.
examples.outcome: Running Bellman-Ford detects any cycle where the sum of $-\ln(r)$ is negative (meaning product of rates $> 1$). Tracing predecessors from the $V$-th pass relaxation extracts the exact arbitrage loop.

examples.title: System of Difference Constraints (Scheduling)
examples.scenario: A build scheduler enforces constraints like `task_B <= task_A + 5` and `task_C <= task_B - 8` across 200 tasks.
examples.outcome: Adding a super-source $s$ with 0-weight edges to all vertices and running Bellman-Ford either yields a valid schedule or proves infeasibility via a negative cycle.

tradeOffs.pro: SPFA skips unrelaxed regions of the graph, often running 5–10x faster on sparse road or network graphs.
tradeOffs.con: SPFA still has $O(VE)$ worst-case complexity on adversarial grid/chain graphs and uses extra queue memory.

tradeOffs.pro: Handles negative weights and detects negative cycles natively with ~15 lines of array code and zero priority queue.
tradeOffs.con: $O(VE)$ time is prohibitive on large graphs (e.g., $V = 10^5, E = 5\times 10^5 \implies 5\times 10^{10}$ ops).

tradeOffs.factor: At-Most-K-Edges Constraint (e.g., Cheapest Flights Within K Stops)
tradeOffs.pro: Truncating Bellman-Ford to $K + 1$ passes using a snapshot `prev_dist` array solves $K$-hop shortest paths directly in $O(KE)$.
tradeOffs.con: Forgetting to copy `dist` before each pass lets a single pass chain multiple hops, violating the $K$-edge bound.

failureModes.name: Infinity Overflow on Unreachable Nodes
failureModes.description: Using `Integer.MAX_VALUE` as $\infty$ and computing `dist[u] + w` with negative `w` or positive `w` overflows to negative numbers, corrupting comparisons.
failureModes.mitigation: Always guard relaxation with `if dist[u] != INF` before computing `dist[u] + w`.

failureModes.name: In-Place Mutation in Hop-Bounded Variants
failureModes.description: Updating `dist` in-place during pass $k$ allows edges relaxed later in the same pass to chain $> k$ hops.
failureModes.mitigation: Copy `prev = dist[:]` at the start of each pass when enforcing an exact $\le K$-edge limit.

failureModes.name: Missing Disconnected Negative Cycles
failureModes.description: Starting from a single source $s$ with `dist[s] = 0` only detects negative cycles reachable from $s$.
failureModes.mitigation: To detect any negative cycle anywhere in the graph, initialize all `dist[v] = 0` (equivalent to a virtual super-source).

failureModes.name: Count-to-Infinity in Distributed Routing
failureModes.description: In distributed distance-vector protocols (like early RIP), a broken link causes neighbors to bounce stale distances back and forth slowly.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply split horizon, poison reverse, and a small hop infinity cap (e.g., 16 hops in RIPv2).

commonMistakes: Forgetting to check `dist[u] != INF` before relaxing `(u, v, w)`, which lets unreachable vertices relax negative edges.
Running only $V - 1$ passes when negative-cycle detection is required, skipping the $V$-th verification pass.
Returning the vertex relaxed on the $V$-th pass as being *on* the negative cycle—it may only be *reachable from* the cycle; walk `parent` $V$ times first to land inside the cycle.
Applying Bellman-Ford to an undirected graph with a negative edge—any negative undirected edge forms a trivial 2-vertex negative cycle.
Using Bellman-Ford on large non-negative graphs ($V > 10^4$) where Dijkstra finishes in milliseconds.

sections.content:
## The idea

Bellman-Ford replaces Dijkstra's greedy vertex selection with dynamic programming over path length. Define $d_k[v]$ as the shortest path from source $s$ to $v$ using at most $k$ edges. Starting from $d_0[s] = 0$ and $d_0[v] = \infty$, each pass iterates over every edge $(u, v, w) \in E$ and applies $d[v] = \min(d[v], d[u] + w)$. By induction, after $V - 1$ passes, every simple shortest path is finalized. A $V$-th pass that still reduces any $d[v]$ proves a path of $\ge V$ edges beat all simple paths—which by the Pigeonhole Principle requires a negative-weight cycle.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider 4 vertices `{A, B, C, D}` with source `A` and edges `A->B (4)`, `A->C (5)`, `C->B (-3)`, `B->D (2)`:

1. **Init**: `dist = {A: 0, B: INF, C: INF, D: INF}`.
2. **Pass 1**: Relax `A->B` (`B=4`), `A->C` (`C=5`), `C->B` (`5 + (-3) = 2 < 4`, so `B=2`), `B->D` (`2 + 2 = 4`, so `D=4`).
3. **Pass 2**: Iterate all 4 edges again; zero distances improve (`changed = False`), so the algorithm exits early with `{A: 0, B: 2, C: 5, D: 4}`.
4. **Cycle check**: If we instead added `B->C (1)` (forming `C->B (-3)` + `B->C (1)` = `-2` cycle), Pass 4 (`V`-th pass) would still lower `dist[B]` and `dist[C]`, flagging the negative cycle.

sections.content:
## Reconstructing the negative cycle

When an edge `(u, v, w)` relaxes on the $V$-th pass, vertex `v` is either *on* the negative cycle or *downstream* of it. To isolate the cycle itself, set `x = v` and follow `x = parent[x]` exactly $V$ times; this guarantees `x` lands inside the cycle. From `x`, walk `parent` again until returning to `x` and reverse the collected path.

## Shortest-path algorithm comparison

| Algorithm | Time complexity | Space | Negative weights | Negative cycle detection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| BFS | $O(V + E)$ | $O(V)$ | No (unit weights) | No |
| Dijkstra (binary heap) | $O((V + E)\log V)$ | $O(V)$ | No | No |
| Bellman-Ford | $O(VE)$ | $O(V)$ | Yes | Yes |
| SPFA | $O(E)$ avg / $O(VE)$ worst | $O(V)$ | Yes | Yes (visit count $\ge V$) |
| Floyd-Warshall | $O(V^3)$ | $O(V^2)$ | Yes | Yes (`dist[i][i] < 0`) |

## Failure modes

- **Silent wrong answer on unreachable nodes**: Relaxing `(u, v, w)` when `dist[u] == INF` if `w < 0` produces `INF + w < INF`, falsely marking unreachable nodes as reachable.
- **Missed cycle outside source component**: Checking arbitrage across disconnected components fails unless all vertices start at `0`.
- **Worst-case latency spike on SPFA**: Adversarial grid graphs trigger $O(VE)$ behavior in SPFA; use standard Bellman-Ford or Johnson's reweighting when inputs are untrusted.

## K-hop constrained variant

For problems like *Cheapest Flights Within K Stops*, you want paths with $\le K + 1$ edges even if a negative cycle exists beyond $K + 1$ hops. Run exactly $K + 1$ iterations, and at the start of each iteration snapshot `prev = dist.copy()`, reading `prev[u] + w` and writing `dist[v]`. That single copy prevents multi-hop cascading within one pass.

## Practical checklist

- Guard every relaxation with `if dist[u] != INF` to prevent integer overflow.
- Add an early-exit `changed` flag to skip redundant passes on sparse graphs.
- Use a `prev` snapshot array whenever enforcing a strict hop limit $K$.
- Initialize all `dist[v] = 0` when searching for *any* negative cycle globally.
- Walk `parent` $V$ times before extracting cycle vertices.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Bellman Ford Shortest Paths

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Bellman-Ford computes single-source shortest paths in $O(VE)$ time by relaxing every edge $V - 1$ times, uniquely supporting negative edge weights and detecting negative-weight cycles.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: V-th Pass Check applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Shortest Paths / Cycle.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Shortest Paths / Cycle experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always guard relaxation with `if dist[u] != INF` before computing `dist[u] + w`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use Bellman-Ford when edges can have negative weights or when you need to detect negative cycles (such as currency arbitrage); otherwise, Dijkstra's $O((V+E)\log V)$ is far faster.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to check `dist[u] != INF` before relaxing `(u, v, w)`, which lets unreachable vertices relax negative edges.
Avoid trap: Running only $V - 1$ passes when negative-cycle detection is required, skipping the $V$-th verification pass.
When to reach for it: Directed graphs containing negative edge weights (e.g., rebates, elevation/energy recovery, difference constraints $x_j - x_i \le w$).
When to reach for it: Detecting negative-weight cycles, such as currency exchange arbitrage where $\prod r_i > 1$ becomes $\sum (-\ln r_i) < 0$.

putItTogether.title: Putting Bellman Ford Shortest Paths Together
putItTogether.summary: Use Bellman-Ford when edges can have negative weights or when you need to detect negative cycles (such as currency arbitrage); otherwise, Dijkstra's $O((V+E)\log V)$ is far faster.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Bellman Ford Shortest Paths before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Running Bellman-Ford detects any cycle where the sum of $-\ln(r)$ is negative (meaning product of rates $> 1$). Tracing predecessors from the $V$-th pass relaxation extracts the exact arbitrage loop.
